english.html: that in criminal matters, where the peril is greater (for it concerns the honour and the life of a man), the witnesses must be presented and offered personally to the judge <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>.

notes.citation: Novels (the Authenticum), collation 7, the title De testibus (Nov. 90), at the paragraph Haec omnia — the passage which, having regulated written testimony for pecuniary causes, requires that in criminal causes the witnesses be produced in person before the judge; and the Authentica Apud eloquentissimum, the Novel-derived note inserted in Code 4.21 (De fide instrumentorum), on the same point (chapter and paragraph numbers unverified)
notes.original: P. hæc omnia. aux nou uelles de Inſt. Sous la vij. collatiõ, aut. apud eloquen tiſſimum. C. de fid. inſtr.
notes.gloss: Aux nouuelles de Inſt. = in Novellis Iustiniani; aut. = Authentica. The authenticae inside the Code are the short updating notes described in the case file §6.2.

english.html: Afterwards the said de Rols is made to come, who, as soon as she had cast her eyes upon the said newcomer, all in tears, and trembling like the leaf shaken by the winds, having her face all bathed in tears, ran to embrace him, asking his pardon for the fault which, through imprudence, and overcome by the seductions, impostures and wiles of the said du Tilh, she had committed.

To understand whether this fault was excusable in the said de Rols, it must be presupposed that, as all other human actions are either voluntary or involuntary <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, so crimes too are committed either voluntarily or not voluntarily <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. Crimes voluntarily done are those which are executed with a deliberate purpose of committing them <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>, as to kill a man by lying in wait <sup class="mk" data-key="d2">d2</sup>, to rape a woman, to steal, to bear false witness, and the like things, which are not committed without fraud and evil intention <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>: and after the execution they are unpardonable and irremissible as regards men <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>, even though he who has committed the act afterwards repents of it <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. Otherwise, no one would ever be punished. For who is he that, to avoid death, corporal penalty, or ignominy, would not say, "I repent"? Those crimes also may be said to be committed voluntarily which are executed through some anger and sudden passion, as if I should kill him whom I find abusing my wife <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>, or who sets himself to kill me <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>.

notes.citation: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book I as printed; the division of actions into voluntary and involuntary is at III.1 (1109b30 ff.)
Digest 1.3.1–2 (De legibus senatusque consultis, l. 1 Papinian, l. 2 Marcian)
notes.original: l. j & ij. D. de legib.
notes.gloss: D. 1.3.1 defines law as, among other things, delictorum quae sponte vel ignorantia contrahuntur coercitio — "the restraint of offences committed voluntarily or by ignorance"; D. 1.3.2 gives Demosthenes' and Chrysippus' definitions.

notes.citation: Digest 48.19.11 (De poenis, l. Perspiciendum, Marcian — Respiciendum is the incipit as the medieval texts read it), § 2, the last paragraph
notes.original: l. reſpiciendum. P. final. D. de pœn.
notes.gloss: Delinquitur autem aut proposito aut impetu aut casu — offences are committed by design, by impulse, or by chance: Coras's whole threefold scheme in this annotation. The P. is the print's sort for §.

notes.citation: Liber Sextus, V.4 (De homicidio voluntario vel casuali), c. 1 (au vj. = in VI, the Sext; chapter content unverified)
notes.original: l. j. C. de homicid. au vj.
notes.gloss: The print's l. and C. are the civil-law sigla, but au vj. marks the Sext of Boniface VIII, whose title De homicidio is V.4; cf. the case file §6.2 on in VI.

notes.citation: Digest 48.5 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis coercendis), the penultimate law (fragment not identified)
Code 1.4 (De episcopali audientia), l. 3; and Decretals X 5.12 (De homicidio voluntario vel casuali), c. 1 (chapter content unverified)
notes.original: l iij. c. de epiſ. au c. i. c. de homicid. aux Decretales.
notes.gloss: Aux Decretales marks the second citation as the Liber Extra; the first c. is the Code.

notes.citation: Digest 47.2.66 (De furtis, l. Qui ea mente, Maecianus; 47.2.65 in some editions); and Decretals X 2.1 (De iudiciis), c. Cum non ab homine (cf. X 2.1.10)
notes.original: l. qui ea mẽte. D. de fur. c cum non ab hom. de Iud.
notes.gloss: Qui ea mente alienum quid contrectavit ut lucrifaceret, tametsi mutato consilio id domino postea reddidit, fur est: nemo enim tali peccato paenitentia sua nocens esse desinit — "no one ceases to be guilty of such an offence by his repentance": Coras's point exactly.

notes.citation: Code 9.9.4 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis, l. Gracchus, Alexander Severus)
notes.gloss: Gracchus, caught in adultery by night and killed by Numerius: the husband who kills the adulterer is not punished as a homicide if the man was of the condition the lex Iulia allowed to be killed.

notes.citation: Digest 1.1.3 (De iustitia et iure, l. Ut vim, Florentinus); and Gratian, Decretum, the last chapter of Distinctio 35 as printed (unverified; the c. final. of D. 35 does not obviously treat self-defence, and the number may be a wrong sort)
notes.original: l. vt vim. D. de iuſt. & in c. final. xxxv. diſt.
notes.gloss: Ut vim atque iniuriam propulsemus… iure hoc evenit, ut quod quisque ob tutelam corporis sui fecerit, iure fecisse existimetur — what a man does in defence of his body he is held to do lawfully.
